MPL_149_001-090_notes.md:218:The option “sans se donner une clôture alg. $\bar K$” replaces a fully pointed field by a field with only a fixed constant embedding. `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scans 022–024, makes the corresponding distinction between pointed schemes, paths, and isomorphism classes, so this is a reformulation of the same choice of morphism equivalence relation. The relative inner-conjugation convention in reconstruction statements must follow that choice; quotienting by all arithmetic conjugations would forget more than quotienting by the geometric kernel.

MPL_149_091-136_notes.md:207:At scan 106, display (4) and its following sentence, “la clôture alg. de $k(x)$ dans $\Omega$” accompanies a canonical comparison whose first subscript remains $\alpha$ or $X$. This **adds** a larger separably closed field of a base point to **LM_140-2_text.tex, scan 22**, which describes a separable residue-field closure, and scan 108 of the present manuscript itself explicitly says “clôtures séparables dans $\Omega$”. Finite étale residue extensions factor through the separable algebraic closure inside $\Omega$, giving the fibre-functor comparison for the fixed scheme $X$ (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., Lemma 58.6.3, Tag 0BQ8), but a merely separably closed $\Omega$ need not contain an algebraic closure in the purely inseparable sense. Confidence: high in this distinction, medium in the intended terminology, and low in the marked subscript; it does not assert invariance of $\pi_1(X_\Omega)$ under changing the base field of $X$.

SECTIONS_STATE.md:80:**Grothendieck's state; published versions.** The letter to Tate (Pisa, May 1966) is the founding text of crystalline cohomology: it names crystals and conjectures that de Rham cohomology is a crystal [V: Illusie quotes it]. Grothendieck developed it in IHES lectures in November–December 1966, published as "Crystals and the de Rham cohomology of schemes" (notes by Coates and Jussila) in *Dix exposés sur la cohomologie des schémas* (1968; Circle copy https://webusers.imj-prg.fr/~leila.schneps/grothendieckcircle/DixExp.pdf) [V reference; link checked]. Barsotti–Tate groups: ICM Nice 1970, "Groupes de Barsotti-Tate et cristaux" (https://webusers.imj-prg.fr/~leila.schneps/grothendieckcircle/GroupesB-T.pdf) and the Montréal lectures, *Groupes de Barsotti-Tate et cristaux de Dieudonné*, SMS 45 (1974) [V reference in Illusie]. His letter to Illusie of 2–4 December 1969 on deformations of Barsotti–Tate groups was written up by Illusie, "Déformations de groupes de Barsotti-Tate, d'après A. Grothendieck", Astérisque 127 (1985), http://www.numdam.org/item/AST_1985__127__151_0/ [title checked]. The 1965 letter in cote 5 concerns a simplification of the proof of the étale duality theorem, not crystals [V].

SECTIONS_STATE.md:111:**Grothendieck's state; published versions.** EGA I–IV appeared 1960–67; EGA V–XIII were never written. The EGA V prenotes date from the 1960s (first numbered EGA IV §§16, 17.15–17.16, 20) and were given to Piotr Blass in 1987 [V: Circle pubtexts; CSG L48d, https://csg.igrothendieck.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/L48d.pdf]. A CSG transcription of "Réflexions sur le plan des EGA" (1960s, source not stated) gives the planned chapters V–XII: projective morphisms; construction techniques; group schemes and torsors; Picard schemes; residues and duality; intersections and Riemann–Roch; étale cohomology (two chapters) [V], https://csg.igrothendieck.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/U90d.pdf.

MPL_146_001-099_notes.md:1101:The inserted characteristic-zero assumption has a visible role in the context’s argument: principal units 1+m are divisible, so changing a uniformizer by such a unit does not change the section class. In characteristic p, 1+t in F_p[[t]] has no pth root, and that particular independence argument cannot be repeated unchanged. A proposed extension should first formulate a tame or prime-to-p version and then separately address wild ramification, rather than silently deleting the insertion.

MPL_146_001-099_notes.md:1156:The equation celebrated as “équation du monogone, victoire !” can be linked directly to the context’s cover y²=x(x−1): set x=−(z−1)²/(4z) and y=(z²−1)/(4z). Then x−1=−(z+1)²/(4z), so y²=x(x−1) by multiplication, with ramification over 0 and 1 and simple poles over infinity. This identifies the displayed rational map with a parametrization of the same quadratic cover that LM 140-2 describes as a spherical map with two monogon faces.

MPL_146_001-099_notes.md:1158:**Confidence:** high. **Reason:** The parametrization and ramification follow by direct substitution and the orders of zeros and poles, independently of ambiguous nearby homography labels.

MPL_146_001-099_notes.md:1171:For the displayed g₂(z)=−(z²−1)²/(4z²), the substitutions z↦−z and z↦1/z leave g₂ fixed and generate a Klein-four group of deck transformations. The fibers over 0, 1, and infinity have respective supports {±1}, {±i}, and {0,∞}, each with multiplicity pattern (2,2), giving total ramification six for a degree-four sphere cover. This provides a short algebraic verification of the bigon construction and a link to the context’s passage between rational covers and cartographic relations, without importing a triangular-face relation into scan 067.

MPL_149_001-090_notes.md:694:The requirement “compatibles aux filtrations modéliques” means that a field-theoretic reconstruction must remember which group quotients arise from which finite-type models, rather than only the limiting absolute Galois group. It adds model-level compatibility to `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scans 025–027, where local punctured discs and their inertia already retain information lost on forgetting the marked model. A useful proof obligation is therefore to reconstruct the specialization and ramification conditions selecting a model, and only then test whether the modelwise morphisms assemble to a field embedding.

MPL_149_001-090_notes.md:778:The predicted “façon de reconstituer les $U=X\setminus\bar I$” asks for more than a recovered set of rational points: finite Galois-stable sets of punctures and their ramification quotients must also be recoverable and functorial. It extends the marked-curve local data in `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scans 025–027, and the equivariant filling constructions in scans 175–179 to a field-first reconstruction intended to avoid breaking the automorphism groups in genera zero and one. A proof must identify which group quotients correspond to filling a chosen finite set and show that these operations commute with finite base extension.

MPL_149_001-090_notes.md:790:The caution “il n'est pas étale sur $X$” correctly distinguishes the normalized completion $X'$ from the universal étale cover of the compactification. It repeats the punctured-local-disc distinction in `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scans 025–027, but now makes ramification part of the global fixed-point formulation. Any comparison with a modern universal-cover construction must therefore use the inverse system of normalizations or compactifications of covers of $U$, retaining the inertia at its boundary, rather than replace $X'$ by an unramified cover of $X$.

MPL_146_001-099_notes.md:800:Own idea: the quotient of opposite vertices in formulas (11)–(13), together with the two poles, is a linear-algebraic model to compare with the dihedrally symmetric sphere of LM_140-2_text.tex, scans 463–465. There the poles are $0,\infty$, the equator is the unit circle, and antipodal pairs of marked points index the “diagonales” that become handles; a Möbius coordinate change sends the real equator of 146 to this unit-circle equator. The geometric comparison is substantive, but the number of punctures and the subsequent handle-gluing operation are extra data, so it does not identify the two surfaces or their groups. Scan 052 later writes conjugation composed with polar symmetry as antipodism, providing an internal continuation of the comparison.

MPL_146_001-099_notes.md:848:The opening sentence attributes two fixed points to $D^{\prime}$, whereas formula (15) uses $\Sigma^{D^+}$ and the later eigenspace discussion makes the distinction consequential. In LM_140-2_text.tex, scan 463, the reflection $z\mapsto1/z$ exchanges the poles $0,\infty$, so the full projective dihedral group preserves the pair but does not fix its two members. Scan 055 of 146 explicitly says that preserving each $P_\omega$ is the condition of coming from $D^+\times\mathbb C^*$, providing a later clarification within the same file. The frozen reading $D^{\prime}$ should remain as written, with $D^+$ or its projective image recorded as the mathematically suggested reading.

MPL_146_001-099_notes.md:1101:The inserted characteristic-zero assumption has a visible role in the context’s argument: principal units 1+m are divisible, so changing a uniformizer by such a unit does not change the section class. In characteristic p, 1+t in F_p[[t]] has no pth root, and that particular independence argument cannot be repeated unchanged. A proposed extension should first formulate a tame or prime-to-p version and then separately address wild ramification, rather than silently deleting the insertion.

MPL_146_001-099_notes.md:1156:The equation celebrated as “équation du monogone, victoire !” can be linked directly to the context’s cover y²=x(x−1): set x=−(z−1)²/(4z) and y=(z²−1)/(4z). Then x−1=−(z+1)²/(4z), so y²=x(x−1) by multiplication, with ramification over 0 and 1 and simple poles over infinity. This identifies the displayed rational map with a parametrization of the same quadratic cover that LM 140-2 describes as a spherical map with two monogon faces.

MPL_146_001-099_notes.md:1158:**Confidence:** high. **Reason:** The parametrization and ramification follow by direct substitution and the orders of zeros and poles, independently of ambiguous nearby homography labels.

MPL_146_001-099_notes.md:1171:For the displayed g₂(z)=−(z²−1)²/(4z²), the substitutions z↦−z and z↦1/z leave g₂ fixed and generate a Klein-four group of deck transformations. The fibers over 0, 1, and infinity have respective supports {±1}, {±i}, and {0,∞}, each with multiplicity pattern (2,2), giving total ramification six for a degree-four sphere cover. This provides a short algebraic verification of the bigon construction and a link to the context’s passage between rational covers and cartographic relations, without importing a triangular-face relation into scan 067.

LM_140-2_notes.md:2006:**R11 — scans 146–147 — unproved claim — keep, corrected: the lemma as written is false.** "Soit u un homéomorphisme d'ordre fini de ℂ, commutant à z ↦ z+1, et laissant invariant l'origine. Alors u = id": u(z) = z̄ satisfies every stated hypothesis and is not the identity (N4). The application has Γ = Γ°, so what is needed is the lemma for orientation-preserving u; N5 gives a route.

LM_140-2_notes.md:2046:**N4 — scans 146–147 — Own (second pass), counterexample to the stated lemma.** u(z) = z̄ is a homeomorphism of ℂ of order 2, commutes with z ↦ z + 1 (conj(z + 1) = z̄ + 1) and fixes 0, yet u ≠ id. So the lemma as written ("Soit u un homéomorphisme d'ordre fini de ℂ, commutant à z ↦ z+1, et laissant invariant l'origine. Alors u = id") is false; it needs "u conserve l'orientation", which holds where it is used (Γ = Γ°, scan 146). The sentence "Il reste à prouver que si un groupe fini Γ opère sur ℂ en commutant à l'action de ℤ …" has the same gap. Confidence: high (direct check).

LM_140-2_notes.md:2473:**R07 — scan 193 — claim without proof — correct.** With the inserted word the lemma reads "Tout automorphisme direct extérieur u d'ordre fini n d'un groupe à lacets π, qui fixe une classe de lacets i et est tel que l'extension de ℤ/nℤ par Lᵢ ∈ i définie par u soit triviale, est trivial." The hypothesis "direct" (orientation-preserving) is part of the statement (CSG/IUT agree); the first pass had misread the inserted word as a margin "évident!". The lemma is admitted on scan 196, not proved.

MPL_146_100-134_notes.md:58:The replacement of the indexing category by an “ens. ordonné” is asserted after the insertion “rigide,” but the unfinished sentence does not state precisely which ends are individually fixed. For a stable tree with individually labelled leaves, each internal edge determines a leaf bipartition, providing a route to eliminating automorphisms; a proof must also show uniqueness of the relevant contraction maps, since absence of automorphisms alone does not make a category a poset. This **adds to** `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scan 88, whose Boolean-poset axiom concerns quotients of one fixed graph, and scans 99–100, which discuss ordered sets of normalization morphisms; neither is automatically the refinement category left unfinished here.

MPL_146_100-134_notes.md:214:The inference from a uniquely determined three-pointed projective line to “$M_G$ est la multiplicité ponctuelle” is correct only for the graph-pinned moduli problem with the three special points individually identified. Forgetting the pinning can retain graph automorphisms even though every rational component has no automorphism fixing its three labels, so a geometric point is not automatically the same object as a point stack. A proof should reconstruct the curve from the labelled normalization and paired branches, then check morphisms and descent, not merely uniqueness over $\mathbb C$. **Context—restates, with a crucial qualification made explicit elsewhere:** searches for modular dimension zero and unique isomorphism locate `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scan 52, which writes $M_G\simeq\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z$ but $M_{[G]}\simeq B\Gamma$, and scan 55, which identifies the automorphisms recovered after forgetting pinning.

MPL_146_100-134_notes.md:218:The words “homogène unique invariante” must be read together with the subsequent choice of radius $1$: invariance under the finite permutation group alone does not determine an arbitrary positive metric. A direct proof for the normalized round metric is to map the labelled triple by a Möbius transformation to an equilateral triple on the unit sphere; every permutation of that target triple is induced by a rotation, so the pulled-back round metric does not depend on the ordering used, whereas multiplying a metric by a nonconstant invariant positive function shows why unrestricted invariance is insufficient. For uniqueness within normalized round conformal metrics, the order-three subgroup makes the marks a latitude orbit, while a conjugating involution reverses that latitude and hence forces it to be the equator; the three marked points then determine the conformal identification uniquely, whereas an unrestricted invariant metric need not be round. **Context—restates the sphere symmetry and adds metric normalization:** the sphere/permutation search gives `LM_140-3_text.tex`, scans 85–86, with an equator, meridians, twelve spherical triangles, and the $\mathfrak S_3\times\mathbb Z/2$ action; those pages do not formulate this metric uniqueness.

MPL_146_100-134_notes.md:338:The claimed “isom canonique” $T_i\simeq\mathbb U\times_{\mu_2}\omega_Q$ can be checked by sending either orientation of the square to its directed tangent ray at $i$ along the circle through its vertices. Reversing that orientation multiplies the ray by $-1$, and the uniquely determined square rotation carrying one vertex to another transports the rays, giving the required compatibility of the four torsors and the diagonal sign action on their product. This **adds a finite symmetry reduction to** the circles of tangent half-rays and their universal covers in `LM_140-4_text.tex`, scans 225–226 and 255; searches for tangent rays, square structures, and torsors found no exact contextual $\omega_Q$-reduction.

MPL_146_100-134_notes.md:414:The phrase “à isom. unique près” should be assessed for the quotient together with its specified contraction from $G$, since the target graph taken alone can have nontrivial automorphisms. **Context—restates:** `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scans 42–47, constructs the same quotient and expresses its universal property as a pushout in generalized graphs before stating uniqueness of the resulting contraction. In the present formulas, the target vertex set, retained flags, involution, incidence map, and genus weights are all forced by $G$ and $C$; the corresponding later definition is Getzler and Kapranov (1998, §2.14).

MPL_149_001-090_notes.md:74:The assertion “on reconstitue les objets” following the three inverse-limit formulas requires distinct notions of limit: the group formula is an ordinary profinite limit, while groupoids and topoi require their appropriate categorical comparison. Descent of finite étale covers along affine inverse limits supplies the group-level statement with compatible geometric points (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tag 0BTU, Lemma 58.14.1). `LM_140-4_text.tex`, scans 023–024, likewise separates a projective system from the existence of its scheme-theoretic limit; this is an analogous methodological point in a different category, not a proof of the topos formula.

MPL_149_001-090_notes.md:110:The cofinal system of “$A_i$ réguliers” with localization maps can be built by fixing a smooth affine model and then inverting enough nonzero functions to include each finite set of field elements. Smoothness on a dense open in characteristic zero supplies the starting model (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tag 04QM). The closest contextual locus is `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scans 434–435, where models with geometric fundamental groups replace the generic field group; the present page adds the precise cofinal affine presentation required for that passage.

MPL_149_001-090_notes.md:122:The identification in (10), attributed to “résultats bien connus,” follows by descending finite étale covers to a sufficiently small affine model, with all groups based at the same geometric generic point. This is precisely the finite-cover continuity mechanism in The Stacks Project Authors (2026, Tag 0BTU, Lemma 58.14.1). `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scan 434, contrasts the group of a parameter scheme with that of its generic point; the present limit formula adds the relationship between those groups rather than identifying any one model with the generic point.

MPL_149_001-090_notes.md:138:The description as an “extension successive de ... groupes profinis libres” needs affine curve fibres and exactness with an injective fibre-group map, rather than just right exactness of a homotopy sequence. Artin’s elementary fibrations provide punctured smooth curve fibres, but the successive asphericity and completion steps still need justification (Artin, 1973, Exposé XI, §§3–4). `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scan 526, uses a curve $K(\pi,1)$ comparison to control a gerbe obstruction, whereas cote 149 adds an iteration of this mechanism in higher dimension.

MPL_149_001-090_notes.md:327:“on vérifie qu'une variété élémentaire d'Artin se plonge” requires an explicit construction or a precise definition of the elementary class: the universal map to a semiabelian variety need not be an immersion for an arbitrary tower of hyperbolic fibrations. `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scan 064, repeats a curve-based exclusion of projective and affine lines, while `LM_140-4_text.tex`, scan 146, adds the concrete embedding of the three-punctured projective line; neither proves the general embedding asserted here. A reconstruction should separate the curve case from the induction on fibrations and specify where the latter supplies a semiabelian embedding, rather than attributing that conclusion to the universal property alone.

MPL_146_100-134_notes.md:94:The explicit warning “ne sont définies que dans la catégorie homotopique” leaves open which homotopies compare a composite generization with the direct one and which identities those homotopies satisfy. This **differs in presentation from**, but need not contradict, `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scans 82 and 87: the former uses a 2-cartesian diagram and the latter packages transitivity as functoriality. A useful reconstruction would retain chosen natural isomorphisms and verify coherence before passing to a strict presentation; the simply-connected moves complexes of Hatcher and Thurston (1980) and Bakalov and Kirillov (2000) explain why relations among elementary moves are relevant, without identifying those complexes with the present one.

MPL_149_091-136_notes.md:89:The observation that the closed-point fields are “extensions finies de ce $k$” permits $G_{k(s)}$ to be identified with an open subgroup of $G_k$, after compatible embeddings of separable closures have been chosen. This restates the warning in `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scan 73, that the residue algebraic closure is not canonically the previously chosen closure of the ground field. Taking the complete regular curve model organizes its places intrinsically, but does not remove the conjugacy choice of a lift $s^{\prime}$ or supply a preferred splitting of $D_{s^{\prime}}\to G_{k(s)}$ (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., Tag 0BSD). Consequently the current formulas should be compared as compatible based constructions or as conjugacy classes, according to which choices have been fixed.

MPL_146_001-099_notes.md:1101:The inserted characteristic-zero assumption has a visible role in the context’s argument: principal units 1+m are divisible, so changing a uniformizer by such a unit does not change the section class. In characteristic p, 1+t in F_p[[t]] has no pth root, and that particular independence argument cannot be repeated unchanged. A proposed extension should first formulate a tame or prime-to-p version and then separately address wild ramification, rather than silently deleting the insertion.

MPL_146_001-099_notes.md:1156:The equation celebrated as “équation du monogone, victoire !” can be linked directly to the context’s cover y²=x(x−1): set x=−(z−1)²/(4z) and y=(z²−1)/(4z). Then x−1=−(z+1)²/(4z), so y²=x(x−1) by multiplication, with ramification over 0 and 1 and simple poles over infinity. This identifies the displayed rational map with a parametrization of the same quadratic cover that LM 140-2 describes as a spherical map with two monogon faces.

MPL_146_001-099_notes.md:1158:**Confidence:** high. **Reason:** The parametrization and ramification follow by direct substitution and the orders of zeros and poles, independently of ambiguous nearby homography labels.

MPL_146_001-099_notes.md:1171:For the displayed g₂(z)=−(z²−1)²/(4z²), the substitutions z↦−z and z↦1/z leave g₂ fixed and generate a Klein-four group of deck transformations. The fibers over 0, 1, and infinity have respective supports {±1}, {±i}, and {0,∞}, each with multiplicity pattern (2,2), giving total ramification six for a degree-four sphere cover. This provides a short algebraic verification of the bigon construction and a link to the context’s passage between rational covers and cartographic relations, without importing a triangular-face relation into scan 067.

MPL_146_001-099_notes.md:327:### R023 — The ineffective Klein-four kernel changes isotropy but has no invariant line character

MPL_146_001-099_notes.md:331:My comparison keeps the S₄-mixed and S₃-mixed groupoids distinct because the first retains ineffective Klein-four isotropy. For equivariant line bundles over the connected complex base U₀,₃, however, the Klein-four action on a line is a constant character into {±1}, and conjugation by S₃ forces it to be trivial because S₃ permutes the three nontrivial characters transitively. Thus every S₄-linearized line descends to S₃ and \(\operatorname{Pic}^{S_4}(U_{0,3})\simeq\operatorname{Pic}^{S_3}(U_{0,3})\) in this setting, even though the quotient groupoids and their orbifold invariants differ. The contextual order-six calculation can therefore be compared after this descent argument, which does not follow merely from equality of the actions on the base.

MPL_146_001-099_notes.md:333:**Confidence:** high. **Reason:** The kernel acts by globally constant order-two scalars on a line over the connected complex base; the only S3-invariant character of V4 is trivial, so the linearization factors through the quotient.

MPL_146_001-099_notes.md:451:The present use of \(\mathcal O(1)\) leads to the context’s claimed order-six equivariant class, but the first-pass context simultaneously gives a sixth-power trivialization and says there is no invariant section “pour \(n\le6\)”. The likely endpoint question is \(n<6\) versus \(n\le6\), and the associated invariant-polynomial display is also only first-pass material. These contextual readings should be checked against their own scans before they are used as a proof of a precise order; they supply no authority to change cote 146.

MPL_146_001-099_notes.md:553:Own idea: in the later identification $V^{**}=\mathbb C^2\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^n\Delta_{i,\mathbb C}$ of scans 052–053, choose a linear form $\ell_0$ defining one deleted line and normalize every vector by $\ell_0(v)$. This gives $V^{**}\simeq\mathbb C^*\times(\mathbb C\setminus\{n-1\text{ points}\})$ and hence $\pi_1(V^{**})\simeq\mathbb Z\times F_{n-1}$, with the first generator the full scalar fiber turn. It provides an independent check on the fiber relation “$\mu^\vee\mu=\lambda$,” the rank of the reduced presentation, and any attempt to deduce uniqueness merely from a squared relation, while the chosen deleted line prevents treating this splitting as canonical or dihedrally invariant. LM_140-4_text.tex, scans 264–268, supplies an orientation-module and torsor comparison, but does not state this arrangement product; the abstract fiber-injectivity condition of 146 scan 090 is satisfied here because the punctured sphere has vanishing $\pi_2$.

MPL_146_001-099_notes.md:594:A segment “ne contenant pas l’origine” can still have its supporting line through the origin, for example $x=(1,0)$ and $y=(2,0)$, so that condition alone does not define the stated orientation from a half-plane containing $0$ in its interior. The corollary immediately adds “non homothétiques,” which supplies the needed exclusion of a supporting line through $0$. This is a scope question for the lemma rather than a proposed alteration of the frozen text. Targeted searches found no matching segment lemma in the context; LM_140-2_text.tex, scan 143, is the nearest half-plane and orientation comparison, but concerns invariant conformal structures and does not resolve this omitted hypothesis.

MPL_146_001-099_notes.md:706:The margin calls $n=2$ “très dégénéré,” although its final explanation remains uncertain. Own idea: after projectivizing the $2n$ vertices to $n$ marked points, this case gives a twice-punctured sphere, whose Möbius automorphism group preserving the pair is $\mathbb C^*\rtimes C_2$, whereas a configuration of at least three distinct marked points has finite automorphism group. This explains a genuine failure of recovering the same finite dihedral structure from projective marked data, even though the Euclidean square itself and its invariant metric cause no difficulty. ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex, scan 017, also explicitly eliminates genus zero with at most two markings, so the present exclusion adds a concrete geometric counterpart to that stability boundary rather than establishing the intended reading of the margin.
MPL_146_001-099_notes.md:772:### R055 — Uniqueness of the normalized invariant quadratic form

MPL_146_001-099_notes.md:776:The claim of an “unique forme quadratique” invariant even under $D^+$ and equal to $1$ at the vertices can be proved by averaging any positive form over the finite rotation group and then comparing invariant symmetric forms. A nontrivial planar rotation through an angle other than $\pi$ has only scalar symmetric operators in its commutant, so all invariant forms are proportional and the vertex normalization fixes the scalar. The hypothesis $m=2n\ge6$ ensures the required rotation, and the same proof also works for the excluded square $m=4$. LM_140-2_text.tex, scans 142–143, seeks invariant conformal structures for finite plane actions; these pages add the stronger uniqueness statement available for this specific linear representation.

MPL_146_001-099_notes.md:1308:Assume L_i is the tangent line at the i-th marked point and L=⊗_iL_i carries its natural S₅-equivariant structure, as suggested but not fully defined on these sheets. At the configuration {1,i,−1,−i,∞}, z↦iz cycles the four finite points and fixes infinity, acting on their tensor product with multiplier i⁴·i⁻¹=−i, hence with multiplier −1 on L⁶. Consequently an everywhere nonzero S₅-invariant trivialization of L⁶ is impossible under those conventions; replacing every tangent line by its dual reverses the character but preserves its order four. This is a direct test of the conditional interpretation, not a resolution of the uncertain exponent glyph or of all the table’s exact orders.

Deligne and Mumford (1969, Theorem 5.2) provide the normal-crossing boundary framework for their stable-curve stacks, while Keel (1992, Catalogue, Facts 1–4) makes the genus-zero boundary products and intersections explicit; neither citation by itself substitutes for checking the precise marked products used here.

MPL_147_048-137_notes.md:506:For this finite union of connected boundary divisors, the proposed argument is equivalently the connectedness of the graph joining two divisors when their intersection is nonempty. In genus zero, the edges of this incidence graph can be checked using compatibility of the two marking partitions (Keel, 1992, Catalogue, Fact 4). This proves a statement about connected components; the later fundamental-groupoid programme additionally needs relations among paths, which are not encoded by that incidence graph alone.

MPL_147_048-137_notes.md:554:An adjacent exchange of markings produces two maximal chains whose common edge contraction has a four-pointed rational component. The proof is completed by the connected one-dimensional family of that component and its boundary degenerations, which stays inside the ambient boundary because other nodes remain in the range under consideration; the relevant boundary product descriptions are explicit in Keel (1992, Catalogue, Facts 2–4). Generating all permutations by adjacent exchanges then gives the claimed connectivity, while relations among those exchanges remain a separate issue for the programme beginning on scan 076.

MPL_147_048-137_notes.md:100:The equivalence rests on nonnegativity of every stable vertex contribution \(3g_v-3+n_v\): a zero sum forces each vertex to be rational with three total special flags. This argument fails without stability, so the preceding extension from MD-graphs to arbitrary “maquettes” on scan 049 must not be silently carried into this classification. It also explains why the zero-dimensional factors can be removed from the product decomposition on scans 056–060.

MPL_147_048-137_notes.md:120:Here a stratum of modular dimension zero can lie in an ambient moduli space of dimension one or two; the drawings record the difference through the number of edges. Keeping both dimensions in a separate graph invariant would prevent the later small-dimensional classification from being read as a bound on the genus of every graph occurring in a boundary stratum. Scan 060's product cases illustrate why small stratum dimension and small ambient dimension should be tested independently.

MPL_147_048-137_notes.md:126:“On voit” compresses a useful classification argument: with one topological cycle, total marking weight at most two, and rational trivalent decorated vertices, an attached tree consumes at least two markings at its terminal vertex. This leaves either the loop with one marked vertex, the two-vertex cycle, or the loop with a terminal rational component shown on the page. The argument should count loop half-edges twice and distinguish topological type from combinatorial subdivision, as in scan 053.

MPL_147_048-137_notes.md:146:The classification follows from solving \(3g-3+n=1\) and \(3g-3+n=2\) under \(2g-2+n>0\), and from expressing one or two as sums of nonnegative vertex dimensions. It would also clarify that the loop contribution belongs in the total flag count \(n\), not in the vertex genus before contraction.

MPL_146_100-134_notes.md:9:Each item has one of the requested classifications: **conjecture**, **unproved claim**, **unpursued implication**, **own idea**, or **reading question**. The classification “conjecture” includes an explicit question or expectation written by Grothendieck, without suggesting that he states it as a formal conjecture. “Unproved claim” means that the present pages do not supply the indicated justification; it does not imply that the claim lacks a known proof. Confidence assessments concern the stated deduction or proposed construction, and do not assert novelty or historical priority. Statements involving stacks or orbifolds use their classifying-space homotopy types unless specified otherwise.

MPL_147_138-190_notes.md:200:The claim that the “donnée … est équivalente” to compatible subsets of $\pi_0(D_d)$ makes the admissible closed $\Sigma$ recoverable from the global component data rather than arbitrary local labels. This **adds** a closed-subset classification to the branch-labeling torsors of `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scans 109 and 117, where permutation monodromy is already built into the flag spaces. To prove both directions one must show that the component selections respect the incidence maps and descend to a locally finite union of branch intersections, and that every such union yields exactly those selections. Working with $\pi_0(D_d)$ incorporates the global branch identifications; independently labeling local branches without their transport could produce a selection that does not descend.

MPL_147_138-190_notes.md:204:The description “c’est donc un crible” claims that the selected analytic subcategory is full and closed under every arrow whose target lies in it. This **restates** the source/target and composition formalism of `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scans 113–114, but **adds** the equivalence of such componentwise subcategories with admissible closed subsets. The direction of closure is essential: (250) selects arrows by their targets, and (251) ensures that their sources are also selected, so every surviving flag is determined by its final object together with its incoming chain. The equivalence should therefore be read with the analytic and component-selection conditions retained, rather than as a classification by arbitrary abstract subcategories of the incidence category.

MPL_147_138-190_notes.md:288:The relative “pièces de construction” suggest testing a description by exit-path data that retains directed specialization and its homotopies, rather than using only the separate fundamental groupoids of the pieces. This proposal **adds** a possible organization of the flag tubes to the noninvertible recollement transformation of `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scans 164–165, while respecting that file’s distinction, on scan 166, between the mixed topos and its galoisian reflection. Treumann’s exit-path classifications supply comparison targets under conical-stratification and tameness hypotheses; identifying these germ flags with exit paths remains a separate task (Treumann, 2009, Theorems 1.2 and 7.14). Confidence is medium because the needed specialization data are present in the program; constructing the comparison and checking the stratification hypotheses remain necessary, and scan 180 rules out concluding that a constructible category of sets alone recovers the ambient homotopy type.

MPL_147_138-190_notes.md:302:“On s’attend” explicitly makes the proposed description of all elementary topoi by products of the four rank-one models an expectation. The page **adds** a topos-level product claim to `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scan 106, where the branch set and its Boolean lattice describe only the local normal-crossing incidence structure. A proof must show both that each proposed product has the intended intrinsic neighborhood meaning and that coordinate changes preserve the resulting objects and morphisms. The $4^{|I|}$ count is consequently a count in a labeled coordinate model, not yet a classification of globally distinct canonical topoi.

MPL_147_138-190_notes.md:390:The “tore tordu convenable, que je me dispense d’expliciter” can be compared with the already explicit branch-permutation construction $T_d$, $G_d$, and $P_d$. Thus the page **restates** the descent mechanism of `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scans 121–123, while **adding** its proposed application to the filtered subquotients. For a selected block of branches, one should descend the product of their scaling groups and the product of their punctured normal lines together, rather than infer a canonical torus from an arbitrary local splitting of a vector bundle. The character-sheaf classification in Conrad (2014, Appendix B, Proposition B.3.4) supplies the algebraic comparison framework; applying it to the analytic branch construction still requires specifying the relevant local system and its descent data.
